title: Carpet in Lynnwood Condos: Sound Requirements and HOA Rules
meta: Carpet in Lynnwood condos: what HOA sound rules (IIC ratings, coverage rules, work hours) really require, which pad passes, and how to get approved. Wills Flooring.
keywords: condo carpet HOA rules, IIC rating carpet condo, condo flooring sound requirements, carpet padding for condos, carpet installation Lynnwood WA

blocks.lead: Most Lynnwood condo HOAs require carpet or an equivalent sound-rated floor over a set share of the unit, set a minimum impact sound rating for the assembly, and ask for written approval before any flooring work starts.
blocks.detail: Carpet over a dense pad is the easiest floor in the building to get approved because it beats almost any sound rule on its own. The work is in reading your CC&Rs, picking a pad the board recognizes, and scheduling around quiet hours and elevator rules.

blocks.html: Lynnwood has more condo and townhome units than it did five years ago, and most of them sit within a few blocks of our showroom on 196th. The buildings around the City Center and Alderwood, the older stacked-flat complexes off 44th, and the new mid-rises by the light rail station all have one thing in common: a neighbor below who can hear your floor. That is why the HOA cares what you install. This post explains what the rules usually say, what the sound numbers mean, and how to get carpet approved and installed without a letter from the board.

blocks.text: What Lynnwood HOA flooring rules usually say

items.title: A coverage requirement
items.text: Many stacked buildings require that a percentage of the unit's floor, or specific rooms such as bedrooms and living areas, stay carpeted or covered with an approved soft surface. Kitchens and baths are normally exempt. Some older Lynnwood complexes require carpet in every room except those two.

items.title: A minimum sound rating
items.text: The rule is usually written as an IIC number for the floor assembly, commonly 50 or higher, sometimes with an STC figure for airborne sound too. Carpet over pad clears an IIC of 50 easily, which is why most boards do not even ask for a test report on carpet.

items.title: An approval process
items.text: Expect an architectural request form, a product spec sheet, the pad spec, the installer's license and insurance, and sometimes a neighbor sign-off. Approval can take one meeting cycle, so start weeks before you want the floor in.

items.title: Work rules
items.text: Weekday hours, an elevator reservation with pads, a deposit for the loading zone, and a rule about where the old carpet goes. Ground-floor units and townhomes near Martha Lake face fewer of these because there is nobody below.

blocks.note: IIC measures impact sound such as footsteps; STC measures airborne sound such as voices. Ranges are typical lab figures for wood-frame construction, not a guarantee for your building. Concrete-slab mid-rises start higher.

blocks.text: Which pad passes the board and which one wears out

a.title: Dense rebond or felt, 7/16 in or thinner
items: High density rating is what boards and carpet warranties look for
Firm enough for stairs and traffic lanes inside the unit
Adds a large IIC margin over any hard floor
Felt and fiber pads add a little STC benefit as well
Spec sheet is easy to attach to the approval form

b.title: Thick, soft, low-density foam
items: Feels plush for a season, then packs down and lets the carpet flex
Voids many carpet manufacturer warranties over a set thickness
Sound gain over a proper dense pad is minor
Seams and edges loosen sooner, so the floor needs restretching
Some boards reject anything without a published density figure

blocks.text: Mistakes that get a Lynnwood condo owner a violation letter

items: Installing first and asking later. Boards can require removal of an unapproved floor at the owner's expense. Carpet is easy to approve, so there is no reason to skip the form.
Replacing bedroom carpet with hard flooring because the listing looked better, then discovering the coverage rule. Carpet in bedrooms and hard surface in the living area is the usual compromise.
Reusing the old pad to save a step. Old pad is compressed, may carry pet odor, and often does not match the spec the board approved.
Ignoring quiet hours. Power stretchers and staple guns are loud. We schedule to the building's window, but the owner has to tell us what it is.
Leaving the old carpet roll in the hallway or dumpster area. Most Lynnwood complexes fine for that. Haul-away is part of a proper install.
Forgetting the neighbor downstairs. A short note before install day prevents most complaints to the board, which is where violation letters start.

blocks.title: If you want hard floors instead:
blocks.text: Some Lynnwood boards will approve vinyl plank or hardwood in living areas if the underlayment carries a test report that meets the building's IIC minimum. It is a heavier paperwork lift than carpet and the pad choice is critical. See our notes on hardwood in condos and vinyl plank in condos before deciding.

items.html: Get the actual rule in writing. Ask the manager for the flooring section, not a verbal summary. The IIC number and the coverage share should be in the text.
Ask for the pad's density and thickness on the quote. Those two numbers are what the board checks and what the carpet warranty depends on.
Confirm license and insurance. Nearly every HOA asks. Wills Flooring is licensed and insured and has been working in Lynnwood buildings since 2013.
Measure the elevator and the hallway turns. Carpet arrives in a 12 ft roll. Tight corridors sometimes mean cutting on the loading dock, which is fine if planned.

Pick fiber for the neighbor below as well as for you. A denser, lower pile carpet over a dense pad is quieter and wears better than a soft, tall plush. Our carpet installation page covers fiber choices.
Book with the approval cycle in mind. Boards that meet monthly can cost you four weeks. Get the estimate first so the packet is complete on the first try.

faq.q: Can my HOA force me to keep carpet in my Lynnwood condo?
faq.a: Yes, if the recorded CC&Rs or rules include a coverage or sound requirement. Those documents run with the unit and bind every owner. Most boards allow hard floors in living areas with an approved underlayment, but bedrooms above another unit often have to stay carpeted.

faq.q: What IIC rating does carpet have?
faq.a: Carpet over a dense pad on a wood-frame floor typically tests in the mid 50s to 60s and higher, well above the IIC 50 most Lynnwood buildings require. That margin is why boards rarely ask for a lab report when the request is for carpet; the pad spec sheet is usually enough.

faq.q: Do I need HOA approval just to replace carpet with new carpet?
faq.a: Usually yes, at least a notice. Many buildings treat like-for-like carpet as a minor change that gets fast approval, but they still want the installer's insurance, the work dates and confirmation the pad meets spec. Check the rules rather than assuming.

faq.q: Which carpet pad is best for a condo?
faq.a: A dense rebond or felt pad at 7/16 inch or thinner. Density matters more than thickness for both sound and wear. Very thick, soft foam pads feel good briefly, void many carpet warranties and are sometimes rejected by boards because they lack a published density figure.

faq.q: How long does condo carpet installation take?
faq.a: One working day for a typical one or two bedroom Lynnwood unit, including tear-out and haul-away, provided the elevator is reserved and we can work the building's hours. Larger townhomes with stairs can run into a second morning.

faq.a: We supply everything the board asks of the installer: product and pad spec sheets, our license and insurance certificate, and a written quote with dates. The owner submits the form, since the HOA relationship is yours, but we make sure the packet is complete the first time.
